message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is unusually well grounded for a capital request because we did not rely on vendor brochures. We insisted on a three-day trial with our own cases and pallet patterns, and the results show the cell sustaining at least 14 cases a minute, above our 12-a-minute line rate, so throughput risk is retired. The financial case is built from our actual labour costs and a firm vendor quote, and it pays back in 3.4 years against a four-year hurdle, with redeployment to Line 5 for every displaced operator. Just as important to me is the safety case. We have our own evidence on site: Line 3, which is already automated, had 4 manual-handling injuries last year against 11 on Lines 1 and 2, which shows clearly what automation does for injury rates. Palletising is the hardest job in the plant, and this removes it. I have reviewed the risks around changeovers and pallet quality and both are manageable. This is a sound investment on cost, capacity and safety grounds.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Robotic Palletising on Lines 1 and 2
Operations Engineering, Kestrel Foods, Wrexley Plant, February 2026

1. Purpose
This study assesses whether to replace manual palletising at the end of packing Lines 1 and 2 with two robotic palletising cells, and recommends a course of action to the Plant Investment Board.

2. Current operation
Lines 1 and 2 pack savoury snacks into cases, which are stacked onto pallets by hand at the end of each line. Each line has two palletising operators per shift, and the lines run two shifts a day (06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00), five days a week. That is eight operator posts in total. At a fully loaded cost of £36,500 per operator per year, manual palletising costs £292,000 a year.

Palletising is the most physically demanding task on site. Operators lift around 4,000 cases per shift, and the task accounts for most of our manual-handling injuries.

Under the site plan agreed by the Board in December 2025, Lines 1 and 2 will move to a single day shift from January 2027, as volume consolidates onto the new high-speed Line 5.

3. The proposed solution
Each cell consists of a four-axis robot, a layer-forming conveyor, a pallet dispenser, safety guarding and a stretch-wrapper. One operator per shift would supervise both cells, handle pallet changes and clear faults.

Vendor trial
The preferred vendor ran a three-day trial in January using our actual cases and pallet patterns.

Table 1. Vendor trial results, 12-14 January 2026
Case type | Share of Line 1 and 2 volume | Peak rate (cases/min) | Sustained rate over 8 hours (cases/min)
14 kg catering case | 60% | 13 | 10.5
8 kg retail case | 40% | 16 | 14.0

Our lines run at up to 12 cases per minute. The trial confirmed that the cell sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types, comfortably above our line rate, so the cell will not become a bottleneck.

4. Safety benefit
Line 3 has had an automated case packer and palletiser since 2023. In 2025 it recorded 4 manual-handling injuries, compared with 11 across Lines 1 and 2. Automation clearly reduces injuries, and we expect robotic palletising to cut manual-handling injuries on Lines 1 and 2 by a similar proportion. For context, Line 3 runs the lighter 6 kg multipack cases and operates on a single shift.

5. Costs and savings
Table 2. Financial summary
Item | Amount
Capital: two cells, installed, including guarding and conveyors | £620,000
Annual maintenance contract (two cells) | £36,000
Remaining supervision: one operator per shift, two shifts | £73,000 per year
Current manual palletising cost | £292,000 per year
Net annual saving (£292,000 - £73,000 - £36,000) | £183,000
Simple payback (£620,000 / £183,000) | 3.4 years

The Plant Investment Board's hurdle for automation projects is a payback of four years or less, so the project meets the hurdle with a margin. The three operators displaced on each shift would be offered redeployment to Line 5, which is currently recruiting.

6. Implementation
The vendor quotes a 16-week lead time. Installation would take place during the planned two-week August shutdown, with a further two weeks of commissioning at reduced line speed. We would train two engineering technicians on robot maintenance as part of the contract.

7. Risks
Changeovers to new case sizes require reprogramming, which the vendor will provide for the first year. Pallet quality varies between suppliers, and poor pallets cause faults in automated dispensing; we will tighten our pallet specification before go-live.

8. Recommendation
Robotic palletising on Lines 1 and 2 is technically proven on our own products, removes our most injurious manual task and pays back in 3.4 years, within the Board's four-year hurdle. We recommend the Board approve capital of £620,000 for installation in the August 2026 shutdown.
</document>
response:
# Review: Robotic Palletising Feasibility Study, Lines 1 and 2

The study does several things well, especially the trial on your own products. But two of its three main claims don't hold up against its own numbers, and the third is overstated. As written, I don't think it should go to the Board.

## 1. The trial shows a bottleneck, not retired throughput risk

The text says the cell "sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types." Table 1 says otherwise:

| Case type | Volume share | Sustained rate | Line rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14 kg catering | 60% | **10.5/min** | 12/min |
| 8 kg retail | 40% | 14.0/min | 12/min |

- **The 14 kg case, your majority product, sustains 10.5/min, below the 12/min line rate.** Only the 8 kg case reaches 14. Its 13/min peak is barely above line rate and wasn't sustained.
- Even a volume-weighted blend (0.6 × 10.5 + 0.4 × 14.0) gives about **11.9/min**, still under line rate. The blend is generous anyway, because a line running catering cases is limited by the cell's rate for that case.
- On catering runs, the cell would cap output at about 88% of line rate. The lost output isn't costed anywhere.

The study needs to state this honestly. Then either show that a fix works (e.g. a vendor configuration change, a different gripper, or a re-run trial) or cost the lost output.

## 2. The financial case ignores the Board's own shift plan

Section 2 notes that Lines 1 and 2 move to a **single day shift from January 2027**. Section 5 still calculates savings on two shifts. With installation in August 2026, the two-shift savings would last only about four to five months.

On a single shift:

| Item | Study (2 shifts) | Single shift |
|---|---|---|
| Manual palletising cost | £292,000 (8 posts) | £146,000 (4 posts) |
| Remaining supervision | £73,000 | £36,500 |
| Maintenance contract | £36,000 | £36,000 (assuming unchanged) |
| **Net annual saving** | **£183,000** | **£73,500** |
| **Simple payback** | **3.4 years** | **~8.4 years** |

Adding the few months of two-shift savings before January 2027 still leaves payback at roughly **8 years, about double the four-year hurdle**. This alone reverses the recommendation, unless there is a reason the single-shift plan won't happen. If so, the study should say so explicitly.

The financial case also leaves out several costs:
- Lost output during two weeks of commissioning at reduced speed
- Reprogramming for new case sizes after the vendor's first year
- Tighter pallet specification, which likely raises pallet cost
- Stretch-wrap consumables
- Technician training time

These are probably small next to the shift issue, but each one pushes payback further out.

On redeployment: moving displaced operators to Line 5 only counts as a saving because Line 5 is recruiting anyway. The study should state that link, since it is what makes the labour saving real.

## 3. The Line 3 injury comparison doesn't support the claimed effect

The study compares 4 injuries on Line 3 with 11 on Lines 1 and 2, and concludes that "automation clearly reduces injuries." But the document itself lists differences that make the two figures non-comparable:

- **Exposure:** Line 3 is one line on one shift. Lines 1 and 2 are two lines on two shifts, roughly four times the line-shift hours. Per line-shift, 4 vs 11 is about 4 vs 2.75. On that basis Line 3 looks *worse*, not better.
- **Load:** Line 3 handles 6 kg cases. Lines 1 and 2 handle 8 kg and 14 kg.
- **No baseline:** there are no figures for Line 3 before automation in 2023, which is the comparison that would actually show an effect.

The underlying point is plausible: removing a task that involves lifting thousands of heavy cases per shift should reduce manual-handling injuries. But the study should argue it from the task itself, using the share of Lines 1 and 2 injuries that come from palletising. The Line 3 comparison should either be normalised for exposure and load or dropped. "Similar proportion" should not be presented as evidence. Note also that Line 3 still has 4 manual-handling injuries after automation, which suggests residual risk from fault clearing and pallet changes that deserves a mention.

## 4. Smaller points

- **Timeline:** the study targets the August 2026 shutdown and it is now November 2026. If this hasn't been approved, the dates, lead time and two-shift window all need updating, and the window has effectively closed.
- **Risk section:** changeover reprogramming beyond year one and dependence on pallet quality are described as "manageable" without owners, costs or fallback plans. The throughput shortfall on 14 kg cases should be the first risk listed.
- **"Technically proven on our own products"** in the recommendation is only true for the 8 kg case.

## What holds up

- Insisting on a trial with your own cases and pallet patterns was the right call, and it is exactly what exposed the 14 kg shortfall.
- The arithmetic in Table 2 is internally correct for the two-shift scenario.
- The case for removing a high-load manual task is reasonable in principle.
- The implementation plan (shutdown install, technician training) is sensible.

## Bottom line

On the study's own data, the cell can't keep pace with the majority product, and on the Board's own shift plan the payback is roughly 8 years against a 4-year hurdle. The safety argument may be the strongest reason to proceed, but it needs honest evidence. I'd suggest reworking the study in one of three ways:
- A single-shift financial case with a throughput fix for 14 kg cases
- A smaller scope, such as one cell or the retail line only
- An explicitly safety-led proposal that acknowledges it misses the payback hurdle
